newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Hanging on word from EU, G7 summits.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Hanging on word from EU, G7 summits.

text.p: The outcome of the Amsterdam summit of European Union (EU) leaders will be key for single currency worriers, while the Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Denver will provide the focus for dollar/yen players next week, economists said on Friday.

"European markets are largely frozen," said Julian Callow, European economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London, as they await concrete news on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from the summit on June 16 and 17.

French and German ministers met on Friday and said they made some progress on reaching a final accord on EU policy coordination for growth and jobs, which has been a stumbling block for an agreement on the stability pact.
An extra meeting of EU finance and economic ministers (Ecofin) has been arranged for Sunday, in advance of the summit.
"That does not look too encouraging -- they are leaving it down to the last minute," said David Brown, senior European economist at Bear Stearns International in London.
Bonn markets will look for a deal to provide an impetus for further convergence, economists said.
Across the globe, G7 leaders will meet on Friday, providing another focus for financial markets after the dollar's roller coaster ride against the yen this week.
"If there is any discussion on the Japanese trade surplus and the growing trade imbalance between the U.S. and Japan, that will focus attention on the dollar," said Brown.
Japanese trade balance data for May will be released on Tuesday and April U.S. trade data on Thursday.
Following an unexpected fall in producer prices released on Friday, markets will home in on U.S. May consumer price data, due on Tuesday.

"The data we have had today will set the market tone for next week," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London, adding that the likelihood was receding of monetary tightening by the U.S. Federal Reserve July's policy-setting committee meeting.
In Europe, the first five of 11 Italian cities will release their preliminary consumer prices data for June on Friday.
"We expect June CPI to come in at 1.5 percent," said Callow.
Italian markets have been looking to a cut in official Italian interest rates for weeks, but low inflation figures will not spark a cut, Callow said.
"The Bank of Italy is clearly going flat out for EMU. It does not want to take any chances of a negative impact on the currency, even though the economy is crying out for a rate cut."
In Germany, May M3 money supply data will be released on Thursday.
"There are expectations of signs of further slowdown in the economy," said Brown.
In Japan, the focus has already switched to the following week, and the release of the crucial "Tankan" survey of corporate sentiment on June 25.
Analysts expect the survey to show worsening sentiment about economic recovery, which could convince the Bank of Japan to hold interest rates steady for a while.
